title: A Room for the Choir
premise: Hospice nurse Sable Quintana has spent years recording the sleep-talk of the dying for a grief-therapy study, and she's heard them all count backwards from ten — always to zero, always before dawn. When a new patient, a mute old woman named Vesper, begins answering questions in her sleep in a voice that is not her own, Sable realizes something at Hollowmere House has been asking the dying for permission. Digging into the hospice's records, she learns that decades ago the staff invited 'the choir' in through a dry well beneath the chapel to ease patients' passing — a bargain renewed every generation by an act of consent no one remembers giving. As the well refills with water on the night of the solstice, Sable must refuse on behalf of everyone who cannot speak, holding out until sunrise while the choir sings her own memories back at her, offering belonging in exchange for her voice. She survives by singing the count backwards herself — turning ten to zero into zero to ten — breaking the invitation, though she wakes with one memory permanently gone: she can no longer remember why she became a nurse.
about_author: Isandro Blackwood is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who claims the worst things he ever saw happened between three and four in the morning. He writes in longhand near open water and refuses to record his own voice.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Introduces Hollowmere House and her ritual of recording sleeping patients; we hear three different dying people count backwards from ten in unison across separate rooms. Sable explains it away as coincidence, establishing her rationalism. Emotional beat: weary competence masking loneliness — she belongs to the dead more than the living.

chapters.title: Vesper Answers
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. New patient Vesper, mute after a stroke, is admitted. Overnight, the recorder captures a second voice asking questions — 'Do you consent?' — and Vesper's mouth moving as she answers yes in her sleep. Sable replays the tape until dawn. Emotional beat: the first crack in her disbelief, and the horror of hearing a question she cannot hear being asked.

chapters.title: What the Well Was For
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, intercut with 1968 logbook entries. She finds the hospice's sealed archives: a dry well beneath the chapel, a founding matron's note about 'easing the passage,' and a list of names ending every generation. The counting, she realizes, is the choir tallying consents. Emotional beat: dread of inheritance — the horror was invited, politely, by people like her.

chapters.title: Ten, Nine, Eight
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. A beloved patient, Mr. Adeyemi, begins counting in his sleep days early, and the second voice starts asking Sable's name through him. Staff begin humming the same tuneless melody without noticing. Her skeptical colleague Ruth dismisses the tapes. Emotional beat: isolation deepening — loyalty to Ruth vs. the truth pulling Sable alone toward the chapel.

chapters.title: The Voice That Knows Me
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The choir stops using patients and speaks directly into the recordings: it recites Sable's childhood, her mother's death, the promise she made at fourteen. It offers belonging — a place in the choir where no one is ever alone again. Emotional beat: temptation; the horror becomes intimate, almost tender, which is worse.

chapters.title: Consent Is a Door
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth secretly listens to the tapes and hears her own dead brother's voice among the choir. Terrified and grieving, she signs a visitor form she doesn't read fully — an act of consent hidden in paperwork. Emotional beat: betrayal born of love; loyalty weaponized against truth.

chapters.title: Seven, Six, Five
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Vesper deteriorates rapidly; the whole ward counts in their sleep now, synchronized. Sable descends into the flooded chapel crypt and finds the well half-full, black water rising, and understands the solstice deadline. The choir tells her sunrise will be too late. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into defiance — she will not answer.

chapters.title: The Renewal
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge on solstice night. Ruth, half-chosen, unlocks the chapel believing she'll see her brother; the staff sleepwalk toward the well singing. Sable physically bars the door, holding it shut as the water rises and the choir counts down through the walls. Emotional beat: climax — one woman's refusal against a building full of surrendered wills.

chapters.title: Zero, Then Sunrise
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. At the count of zero the well crests and the choir enters her mind, offering her mother's voice as the final lure. Instead of refusing silently, Sable sings the count backwards — zero up to ten — reclaiming the numbers, and the invitation collapses at first light. Ruth wakes on the chapel floor, weeping, human. Emotional beat: triumph through reversal; the weapon turned back on its wielder.

chapters.title: A Room for the Choir
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, weeks later. The well is sealed, the recordings archived, the ward quiet — but Sable hums the melody sometimes without meaning to, and one memory is simply gone: why she became a nurse. She keeps a room in her house empty, just in case anything ever needs a place to sing. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution — belonging won, but at the price of a piece of herself left behind in the dark.
